subject: Notes from our memory expert call last Thursday to supplement Hynix. Prices to increase 20-30% next year as HBM makes DRAM even tighter. CXMT tech fears overdone.

body.content:
Hynix was asked about CXMT and LTAs. I had some interesting takeaways from the
chat with Harald Lee last week on those topics and others so sending out the
notes from the call to you all here to supplement the Hynix notes.



_SPEAKER BIOGRAPHY_

 _ _

_Harold Lee is the CEO and Head Semiconductor Industry Advisor at Itz LeeM Co.
(01/2024-present), his own company, which provides semiconductor industry
consulting, technology advisory, and strategic leadership services. Before
this, Lee served as the Senior Vice President of Technology Development and
Manufacturing for DRAM, HBM, 3D NAND, and Logic Foundry at Samsung
(07/2021-01/2024), which develops consumer electronics, semiconductors, and
advanced technology solutions globally and where he had earlier served as
Senior Vice President of Logic Foundry, DRAM, and 3D NAND (12/2015-06/2019)
and Vice President of DRAM amd NAND Flash Research, Development, and
Manufacturing (11/2008-12/2015). Prior to this, Mr. Lee was a Senior Fellow at
Western Digital (06/2019-07/2021), a company producing data storage devices
and flash memory technologies, and the General Manager of Process Integration
at Intel Corporation (12/2000-10/2008)._

** **

**Initial Supply/Demand General Questions**

 _Q To kick things off Samsung and Hynix both say that DRAM/HBM will become
even tighter in 2027 compared to this year. Do you agree and can you discuss
the main factors on both demand and supply side that we need to consider for
2027?_



A

Demand

  * My view for next year is that demand will continue to grow faster than supply. The market will remain tight for HBM and server DRAM. There could be supply demand balance in the CE market due to a decline in demand which has already started. 
  * The production ramp up is more aggressive by NAND makers and Chinese CXMT and YMTC could have a bigger influence next year. On the commodity side mobile and PC we could see this market sluggish but premium pricing for HBM and high end server will remain strong due to strong growth from the AI market. 
  * Next year the market will be more bifurcated between the AI and non AI market. The AI market should continue to see strong demand growth to 2029 or 2030
  * HBM will remain constrained due to the die penalty with consumption continuing. AI workloads require lots more server DDR5 for the server CPU. Also agentic is creating new demand for capacity

Supply

  * On supply DRAM investment takes a long time to set up new clean rooms then the get into ramps. The huge downturn in 2023-2024 meant little capacity has been built. We are only seeing some builds from the middle of last year concerns about oversupply are premature. 
  * Chipmakers only became more confident in expanding capacity a year ago. Clean room and new fabs investments are not made lightly. 
  * Memory fabs cant just turn on need to find the sites then erect the framework and concrete then the fabs are one by one. It typically takes 2 years. But after that there is a lot more work to be done with the equipment delivered. Installation takes 2 months. Then testing takes 6 months. Then wafers can start. It takes 1-1.5 years for yields to mature. Total it takes 3.5 years for supply to come on in full yield. 
  * Cleanrooms can be built but HBM also depends on advanced packaging TSV RDL boding debonding dice thinning underfill and moulding HBM stacking the testing. All of this requires new facilities and teams to deliver on the HBM.  We need a lot more technology and engineering teams for HBM. 
  * SK Hynix said it plans to double wafer capacity for 5 years but said the supply bottleneck could last to 2030. Capacity cant be added to meet supply. 
  * Even with rising wafer output HBM will constrain commodity DRAM. The main makers are directing more capacity to more high end DRAM, HBM and SSD. The trade ratio effect is still in force next year. HBM 4 consumers more than 4x DDR5 capacity compared to 3x for HBM3. It could be 5x with HBM 5. That tightens traditional DRAM capacity which could hlea to more price spikes. 
  * Most reports expect HBM bit shipments of 50-60% yoy. Will be hard to satisfy all the demand for HBM. HBM was 20% last year and will be over 30% next year. 
  * This year the DRAM wafer capacity is 9-13% but bit growth is only 6-7% due to the trade ratio. Adding in node migration bit growth is 16%. 

_ _

_Q How about NAND are technologies such as RAG, vector databases and KV-cache
offload creating a structural change in NAND demand?_

A

  * AI in creating structural increase in eSSD. Before NAND was PC and mobile phones and some traditional DC storage. But new AI workloads require larger faster and more cost effective storage RAG and KV Cache are driving a structural increase in demand for server type NAND. 
  * NAND is more exposed to conventional. DRAM is over 50% with no alternative. NAND is still competing with HDD for the largest market. 
  * Enterprise SSD

![](cid:image001.png@01DD66BF.95D2F4C0)****

** **

**Pricing/LTAs**

 _Q What do you think this means for pricing in Q4 and as we go into 2027?_



A

  * Contract prices have been increasing a lot since Q325. Q126 was more than 90% and another 60% in Q2. 
  * Q3 many reports suggested prices to slow down due to the movements in the spot price. Spot was decreasing in March. That made Trendforce to think 13-18% increase in Q3 and 8-13% in Q4 but that didn’t happen
  * From late Q2 the spot price increased again and continued all the way even now. That has driven increased forecasts it looks like contract prices in Q3 are already up over 20%. And for Q4 nearly 20% increase. 
  * Pricing in memory is already very high its unprecedented Ive never seen this rapid spike in 24 years of my experience. We cant expect a continued rapid spike it cant continue next year
  * Next year will not decrease but there will be a slowdown in the price increase. Maybe 20-30% for the full year for DRAM. That’s due to the HBM trade ratio and die penalty effect. 
  * NAND has no trade ratio effect and it has more players so the overall price will be more muted. NAND could be more supply demand balanced next year NAND could have some saturation in price in 2H27 and some think prices could come down. Maybe from Q2 some think. 



_Q Can you describe the strategies of different vendors in terms of LTAs some
seem to have more price ceilings that others, which ones in DRAM and NAND have
the most potential upside to any further price increases._



A

  * The LTAs are dominant in the server DRAM market. 6 months ago 2/3 of all contracts in server were LTAs already. The server portion is over 50% as high as 60%. 
  * That was 6 months ago now LTAs maybe 80-90% of server contracts are LTAs. 
  * For the full DRAM market LTAs are now 40-50%
  * There are difference in LTA strategy. Samsung’s main advantage is a broad product portfolio and large manufacturing scale and wide product range. Samsung hasn’t disclosed ceilings and floors but think Samsung has good potential for upside for server DRAM and HBM
  * Hynix is more focused  long term customer partnerships in server DRAM and HBM with the likes of Nvidia its more focused on stability and co developing. Hynix has pricing upside but too much volumes are committed already from the past
  * Micron SCA has selling price and floor price as much as 75% this FY Micron gave stronger protection against any price declines but don’t have so much upside from the agreed SCAs. 
  * Not a huge difference amongst the 3 players as we don’t expect a rapid increase in prices but Samsung is more leveraged to it followed by Hynix followed by Micron. 



**China Competition: DRAM**

 _ _

_Q At a recent conference CXMT announced  4F2 and claims it will have DDR5
RDIMM by the end of the year. Do you believe these claims and how competitive
overall is CXMT? Several sources suggest 4F2 on CXMT nodes is still below the
current 6F2 of Samsung and Hynix (CXMT “F” value is 15nm, while the Koreans/MU
are on average at 12.2nm. CXMT cell size is 4*15^2 = 900nm^2 Koreans/MU cell
size is 6*12.2^2 = 893nm^2) is this the right way to think about it?_



A



  * The selloff in the stock market is an overreaction in my view
  * Current DRAM uses 6F2 its just the cell arrangement 4F2 is the most compact arrangement which increases the overall manufacturing process complexity. 33% production in memory cell area would give 50% increase in density on the same node process. 
  * CXMT has made good technical progress and they have introduced different kinds of vertical transistors to get higher density. That was done without EUV. 
  * CXMT is trying to introduce 4F2 before other makers as they don’t have EUV. Samsung Hynix and Micron all have 4F2 technology as well for more than 10 years. They aren’t adopting it yet as they are cautious on new architecture as 6F2 give strong yield. 
  * There is a trade off between yields and process control these vertical transistors in 4F2 require complex litho etching and deposition. Floating body effect is also a big bottleneck. 
  * It also requires some wafer bonding process same as 3D NAND which causes a lot of reliability issues. 
  * So cell performance production cost and manufacturing yield are all in question that’s why global makers haven’t adopted it yet. Its very high risk. They can just introduce EUV instead to reduce the overall cell and dimensions. This is a better approach with lower risk to increase the cell density. CXMT has no EUV so they have no choice but to try 4F2 to progress. 



_ _

![](cid:image002.png@01DD66BF.95D2F4C0)__

_ _

_Conor some extra info on this_

 _ _

_[CXMT IEDM paper: High-Performance GAA Junctionless Vertical-Channel
Transistors for 4F²
DRAM](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14293293&ad=5067943425&h=yYX8a8k&sig=YuuDqJ9i3JZtKkOPQqnYWDCQkWx&v=2&url=https://mys.mapyourshow.com/mys_shared/iedm23/handouts/6-2_Mon_16771.pdf)_

 _ _

_This is authored by CXMT engineers and shows that CXMT has actually
fabricated a junctionless gate-all-around vertical-channel transistor combined
with a capacitor for a compact 4F² DRAM architecture. The paper explicitly
discusses the floating-body effect (FBE) as a problem with conventional
inversion-mode vertical-channel transistors and proposes the junctionless
structure partly to suppress it._

_ _

_[This
paper](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14293293&ad=5067943425&h=yYX8a8k&sig=YuuDqJ9i3JZtKkOPQqnYWDCQkWx&v=2&url=https://mys.mapyourshow.com/mys_shared/iedm23/handouts/6-2_Mon_16771.pdf)
explains why:_

  * _6F² → 4F² requiring a vertical transistor architecture_
  *  _floating-body effect being a major technical hurdle_
  *  _CXMT having done substantive R &D rather than simply announcing a roadmap_

 _ _

_![](cid:image004.png@01DD66C1.0AA15750)___

_ _

_![](cid:image005.png@01DD66C1.0AA15750)___

_ _

_Transitioning to a 4F² DRAM architecture via Vertical Channel Transistors
(VCTs) introduces immense lithography, etching, and deposition
complexities**.** While a 4F² layout theoretically reduces the cell area by
33% compared to standard 6F² structures, flipping the transistor 90 degrees
horizontally into the Z-axis shifts the fabrication burden from simple lateral
scaling to highly complex 3D processing. These manufacturing hurdles are the
primary reason why companies like [Micron
Technology](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14293293&ad=5067943425&h=sz6IH2G&sig=LhtT47DeC0P4dEfMfCQ6sBtvJyx&v=2&url=https://www.micron.com)
abandoned 4F² in late 2026, citing that the extreme process complexity and
cost erode its architectural benefits. Conversely, other manufacturers like
CXMT and YMTC are actively pursuing it to bypass EUV lithography limitations_

 _ _

_[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/371517221_Vertical_Channel_Transistor_VCT_as_Access_Transistor_for_Future_4F_2_DRAM_Architecture](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14293293&ad=5067943425&h=qRw2lrb&sig=WDfQc1C6BWGQaLdCUKtbIkYHNxi&v=2&url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/371517221_Vertical_Channel_Transistor_VCT_as_Access_Transistor_for_Future_4F_2_DRAM_Architecture)_

_[https://patents.google.com/patent/US7521322B2/en](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14293293&ad=5067943425&h=pvtCiLP&sig=W1wedIGVsfLBWSZTXWKmewRTiDq&v=2&url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US7521322B2/en)_

_[https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/vlsi2025](https://jefferies.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14293293&ad=5067943425&h=6vIgYuE&sig=Uv9Nih0q3IfbaMUik8sLpQacQM5&v=2&url=https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/vlsi2025)_

 _ _

_ _

_1 Complex Lithography Challenges_

 _ _

_• Extreme Patterning Density: Reaching a 4F² cell pitch requires defining
dense, regular arrays of nano-pillars at sub-20nm dimensions. Fabs must either
utilize expensive Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography or complex multi-
patterning techniques (like Self-Aligned Quadruple Patterning, or SAQP) using
immersion ArF lithography to resolve the narrow layouts._

_• Critical Dimension (CD) Uniformity: The nano-pillars must feature flawless
CD control (ranging from 5nm to 20nm). Any variations across billions of
pillars on a single wafer directly lead to massive threshold voltage
fluctuations and cell failures._

_ _

_2\. High-Aspect-Ratio Etching Pitfalls_

 _ _

_• Perfect Pillar Carving: Etch tools must cut deep, isolated channels into
the silicon to form the vertical transistor body. This demands highly
isotropic Reactive Ion Etching (RIE) that can achieve perfectly vertical
sidewalls without any micro-loading defects._

_• The Tapering Trap: Real-world etching naturally creates a V-shaped
microscopic taper. A slight taper reduces the physical insulation distance at
the base of the transistor pillar, inducing severe electrical leakage or
outright short-circuiting between adjacent word lines and bit lines._

_ _

_3\. Conformal Deposition & Voiding Risks_

 _ _

_• Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) Constraints: The vertical channel must be
wrapped seamlessly by a gate oxide (often High-k materials like hafnium oxide)
and a metal gate electrode. Fabs rely heavily on ALD to ensure atomic-level
thickness uniformity along the sheer vertical sidewalls._

_• Buried Bit-Line (BBL) Metal Fills: A core element of 4F² is moving the
digit/bit lines underground beneath the vertical pillars. Filling these ultra-
narrow, high-aspect-ratio bottom trenches with ultra-low-resistance metals
(such as Ruthenium or Cobalt) without leaving micro-voids is an extraordinary
material science challenge._

_ _



**China Competition: NAND**



_Q How about the competitiveness of YMTC in NAND they seem to have solid
position in terms of IP with XStacking do you think they can become a global
player or just serve local Chinese demand? Can YMTC get to 400 layers?_



A

  * 10th generation of YMTC should be 430 layers. That increases the number of stacks from double to triple and increase the number of complexity channel etching and high aspect features. 
  * Samsung was targeting 1H26 but has been delayed. They probably wont produce until ear





![](cid:image003.png@01DD66BF.95D2F4C0)





![](cid:image001.png@01DD66BF.95D2F4C0)





_Q Why do you think NAND doesn’t have a trade ratio LAM is talking about SLC
NAND 3 to 1 for agentic as we move back to SLC? ZNAND Samsung and XLFlash from
Samsung we wont know until we see die sizes. Low latency high IOPS for Nvidia
NEXT this is a very custom SLC die a lot more control switches and plains this
will be a much bigger chip than a TCL and SLC. Trade ration for Storage NEXT
could be 4x1 for   SLC to TLC. LAM gave numbers last night. Potentially if
only 5% of the NAND market goes to SLC that’s 15% of the NAND market have you
thought about this for 2027. Overall NAND capacity is not growing at 15%. _

_ _

  * This is too soon to talk about this. SLC is the same process manufacturing as TLC it’s a less sophisticated controller for reading and programme there are only 2 state of the electrical cell. 
  * The same process and same number of wafers the bits would decrease a lot of this happens that’s true 3-4x
  * How much XLFlash will penetrate the market isn’t clear it depends on how Nvidia progresses with storage NEXT but there are other options like HBF from Sandisk. It does something similar in the hierarchy
  * 1-2 months ago HBF looked more promising rather than XLFlash. 
  * HBF trade ratios is even worse stacking could be trade ratio of 6:1. 
  * It takes time for these products to be standardized. 



_Q Micron had a presentation yesterday they said they gave up after 2 decades
of work they are going into 3D instead. Why are they moving to 3D rather than
use EUV?_



  * This shows just how hard to is to give up 4F2. 
  * The original plan wasn’t 4F2 it was 6F2 to 3D monolithic. This also took 10 years of development. But they realized developing all the structure in high volume was harder than expected even more than 4F2. 
  * 3D DRAM is harder than 3D NAND. NAND only has a cell DRAM has cell transistor and must be made on a single crystal. Micron’s goal was to expedite the 3D DRAM from 6F2 that’s why they were so late introducing EUV. Once we move to 3D DRAM don’t need to buy EUV. But then they realized 3D DRAM pull in is really hard. That’s why they inserted 4F2 in between as a time gap before 3D DRAM and end of life of 6F2



_Q Can you talk about the implication of HBM base die from Nvidia NV HBM?_



  * The base die was a controller in the past but from HBM 4 it moves to logic as the role of the base die is enhanced with more focus on performance and a critical device
  * The process node and how its developed impacts pin speed and performance of the HBM
  * We are seeing more customized HBM going forward. Not every customer will do this but many will want to add their own customized functions in the base die. Its harder to do this in the DRAM
  * That’s why there is more co development of the clients and semis design teams its becoming more customized this includes Nvidia, Google, Broadcom, Amazon, they all want customized base die. 
  * The fab process is the same it’s the transistor circuit and interconnect that is different. 
  * The product lines are getting more diversified the product numbers are very different on the HBM.
